L15: cite13†View PDF cite14†HTML (experimental) L16: > Abstract:Open many-body quantum systems play an important role in quantum optics and condensed-matter physics, and capture phenomena like transport, interplay between Hamiltonian and incoherent dynamics, and topological order generated by dissipation. We introduce a versatile and practical method to numerically simulate one-dimensional open quantum many-body dynamics using tensor networks.
L17: It is based on representing mixed quantum states in a locally purified form, which guarantees that positivity is preserved at all times. Moreover, the approximation error is controlled with respect to the trace norm. Hence, this scheme overcomes various obstacles of the known numerical open-system evolution schemes. To exemplify the functioning of the approach, we study both stationary states and transient dissipative behaviour, for various open quantum systems ranging from few to many bodies.

L0@P0: A positive tensor network approach for simulating open quantum many-body systems
L1@P0: A. H. Werner,1 D. Jaschke,2, 3 P. Silvi,2 M. Kliesch,1 T. Calarco,2J. Eisert,1and S. Montangero2
L2@P0: 1Dahlem Center for Complex Quantum Systems, Freie Universität Berlin, 14195 Berlin, Germany
L3@P0: 2
L4@P0: Institute for Complex Quantum systems (ICQ), Universität Ulm, 89069 Ulm, Germany
L5@P0: 3Department of Physics, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, Colorado 80401, USA
L6@P0: Open many-body quantum systems play an important role in quantum optics and condensed-matter physics,
L7@P0: and capture phenomena like transport, interplay between Hamiltonian and incoherent dynamics, and topological order generated by dissipation. We introduce a versatile and practical method to numerically simulate
L8@P0: one-dimensional open quantum many-body dynamics using tensor networks. It is based on representing mixed
L9@P0: quantum states in a locally purified form, which guarantees that positivity is preserved at all times. Moreover,
L10@P0: the approximation error is controlled with respect to the trace norm. Hence, this scheme overcomes various obstacles of the known numerical open-system evolution schemes. To exemplify the functioning of the approach,
L11@P0: we study both stationary states and transient dissipative behaviour, for various open quantum systems ranging
L12@P0: from few to many bodies.
L13@P0: Open quantum systems are ubiquitous in physics. To some
L14@P0: extent any quantum system is coupled to an environment, and
L15@P0: in many instances this interaction significantly alters the system’s dynamics. Traditionally such decoherence processes
L16@P0: are seen as an enemy to coherent state manipulation. However, suitably engineered dissipation can also have beneficial
L17@P0: effects and can be exploited for state preparation [1–6], even
L18@P0: of states containing strong entanglement or featuring topological order [7, 8]. In condensed matter physics, many concepts
L19@P0: such as transport are often studied within the closed systems
L20@P0: paradigm, but, it is becoming increasingly clear that some familiar concepts may have to be revisited in the open system
L21@P0: setting [9], where the interplay between coherent quantum
L22@P0: many-body and open systems dynamics, i.e. the competition between Hamiltonian interactions and dissipation leads
L23@P0: to interesting physical effects. Since few analytical methods
L24@P0: are available for such systems, the design of novel numerical tools for the simulation of dissipative quantum many-body
L25@P0: systems is of the utmost importance. In this work, we present
L26@P0: a new algorithm which captures the open many-body dynamics in one spatial dimension – for both transient and steady
L27@P0: regimes – based on a locally purified tensor network ansatzclass. It comprises a new approach in that the positivity of the
L28@P0: operators is maintained during the whole simulation. Importantly, the approximation errors can be controlled in a way that
L29@P0: yields a trace-norm certificate. Hence, the algorithm provides
L30@P0: not only a conceptually new approach to the problem, but also
L31@P0: combines several desired features of the existing schemes and
L32@P0: overcomes previous limitations.
L33@P0: Tensor-network ansatz-classes have proven to be widely
L34@P0: successful to capture the physics of many-body states [10–
L35@P0: 15]. They rely on the idea that relevant quantum states lie in
L36@P0: the very small sub-manifold with local correlations, which in
L37@P0: turn can be efficiently captured in terms of tensor networks.
L38@P0: The density-matrix renormalisation method [16] can indeed
L39@P0: be viewed as a variational principle over matrix-product states
L40@P0: [11, 13, 17–19]. Generalising these ideas, a number of exciting methods have been proposed [20–26], some of which also
L41@P0: allow to study open quantum systems. In most cases matrixproduct operators (MPO) are at the heart of these methods.
L42@P0: Indeed, several variants have already been developed [27–35],
L43@P0: many of which exploit the well-known features of tensor network ansaetze to encode the mixed many-body quantum states
L44@P0: in a compact matrix-product formulation, ultimately making
L45@P0: the algorithm efficient and stable both for transient [27–29]
L46@P0: and steday state physics [34].
L47@P0: However, in such an MPO description, the resulting truncated operators may not be positive; in fact this property can
L48@P0: not even be locally tested, because it turns out to be a computationally intractable problem [36]. In Ref. [27] this problem
L49@P0: is circumvented by dropping the positivity assumption during
L50@P0: the time-evolution, which requires that the approximation errors remain sufficiently small. Alternatively, quantum jumps
L51@P0: schemes make use of a stochastic unravelling of the master
L52@P0: equation [30, 37, 38] and then employ pure-state techniques,
L53@P0: at the expense of having to sample over many realisations.
L54@P0: Comparative performance of these two approaches has been
L55@P0: recently investigated [39].
L56@P0: Remarkably, the subset of matrix-product operators that are
L57@P0: cast in a locally purified form [27, 40] shows promising features: Such operators are positive by construction and exhibit
L58@P0: all the helpful features typical to tensor networks. However,
L59@P0: while variational algorithms optimising within this class have
L60@P0: been developed for two-dimensional projected entangled pair
L61@P0: states [26, 41, 42] a practical algorithm for one-dimensional
L62@P0: open systems has yet to be formulated. Here we show that
L63@P0: such a positivity-preserving algorithm can actually be engineered for Markovian dynamics: This scheme has the computational efficiency of tensor network methods, allows to control all approximation errors in the operationally relevant trace
L64@P0: norm, and preserves positivity by construction, thus ultimately
L65@P0: merging the advantages of previous techniques while solving
L66@P0: known issues.
